etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sege, from Old French sege, siege, seige (modern French siège), from Vulgar Latin *sēdicum, from Latin sēdicŭlum, sēdēcula (“small seat”), from Latin sēdēs (“seat”).

definitions.definition: (military) A prolonged military assault or a blockade of a city or fortress with the intent of conquering by force or attrition.

quote.citation: 1748, [David Hume], chapter 3, in Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding, London:  […]  A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC, page 5:
quote.text: The Peloponnesian war is a proper subject for history, the siege of Athens for an epic poem, and the death of Alcibiades for a tragedy.

quote.citation: 2001, Alfred S. Bradford, With Arrow, Sword, and Spear: A History of Warfare in the Ancient World‎[1], Praeger, →ISBN, →LCCN, →OCLC, page 145:
quote.text: Liu Pang's general Han Hsin won the strategic city of Hsing-yang for him, but Hsiang-Yü put Liu Pang under siege there.

definitions.definition: (US) A period of struggle or difficulty, especially from illness.

quote.citation: 2012 June 19, Phil McNulty, “England 1-0 Ukraine”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: But once again Hodgson's men found a way to get the result they required and there is a real air of respectability about their campaign even though they had to survive a first-half siege from a Ukraine side desperate for the win they needed to progress.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A seat, especially as used by someone of importance or authority.

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, “ij”, in Le Morte Darthur, book V:
quote.text: Now Merlyn said kyng Arthur / goo thow and aspye me in al this land l knyghtes whiche ben of most prowesse & worship / within short tyme merlyn had founde suche knyȝtes […] Thenne the Bisshop of Caunterbury was fette and he blessid the syeges with grete Royalte and deuoycyon / and there sette the viij and xx knyghtes in her syeges(please add an English translation of this quotation)

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto VII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: To th'vpper part, where was aduaunced hye / A stately siege of soueraigne maiestye; / And thereon sat a woman gorgeous gay […].

definitions.definition: (obsolete) The place where one has his seat; a home, residence, domain, empire.
The seat of a heron while looking out for prey.

quote.citation: 1650, Thomas Browne, chapter III, in Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  A[braham] Miller, for Edw[ard] Dod and Nath[aniel] Ekins, […], →OCLC, 1st book, page 17:
quote.text: Another ground were certain holes or cavities observable about the siege; which being perceived in males, made some conceive there might be also a feminine nature in them.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: Thou art very Trinculo indeed! How cam'st thou / to be the siege of this moon-calf? Can he vent Trinculos?

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: I fetch my life and being / From men of royal siege.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A place with a toilet seat: an outhouse; a lavatory.
(transitive, uncommon) To assault or blockade a city or fortress with the intent of conquering by force or attrition; to besiege.
